blocks.text: Design an MCP server for X has become a real interview question, and it rewards the same instincts as any good system design prompt.
Ask before you assume, name your tradeoffs out loud, and know the difference between a tool, a resource, and a prompt well enough to pick correctly under pressure.
This lesson gives you one repeatable framework you can reuse for any version of this prompt, whatever the domain turns out to be.
1. Why This Question Shows Up in Interviews

blocks.alt: An interview prompt moves from clarifying scope through sorting capabilities to a design

blocks.text: Interviewers like this prompt because it compresses several skills into one conversation at once.
Can you turn a vague product idea into a concrete set of capabilities, and do you understand the security surface a model gains once it can call code for a user.

items: Translating a fuzzy domain into a small, well named set of tools and resources
Reasoning about the security and blast radius of letting a model act on a user's behalf
Handling the realities of a live server, failures, scale, versioning, once it leaves a demo

blocks.text: 2. Clarify the Scope First
Resist naming tools in the first thirty seconds. The most common mistake is designing before anyone has agreed on what the server is for.
Start with who the caller is. An internal coding assistant your team controls behaves very differently from an external host you have never seen.

items: Who is the client, an internal host you control or an arbitrary third party host
What underlying system sits behind this server, a database, a SaaS product, an internal service
Is this read only, or does it also change state, sending messages, creating records, deploying code
What is the expected scale, a handful of daily calls or thousands of concurrent sessions
Does an existing API or SDK already cover this surface, or is this genuinely new

blocks.title: Say your assumptions out loud
blocks.content: If the interviewer will not answer directly, state the assumption you are making and move forward. That reads far better than freezing while you wait for permission.

blocks.text: 3. Identify the Underlying System and Its Constraints
Every MCP server is a thin, standardized layer in front of something that already exists.
Sketch what that system already exposes before you design a single tool, since your job is to expose it well, not to reinvent it.
This step also surfaces constraints early, existing rate limits, an existing auth flow, pagination on large result sets, none of which you want to discover mid design.
4. Tools, Resources, and Prompts, Choosing Correctly

blocks.alt: A capability sorts into a tool, a resource, or a prompt

blocks.text: MCP gives you three primitives, and picking the right one for each capability is the core skill this question is testing.
Tools are for actions or anything whose result genuinely depends on model supplied arguments. Resources are for read only context the model can pull in as data.
Prompts are reusable templates that shape how a task gets approached, useful when a workflow benefits from a consistent, pre written structure.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Primitive","Use it when","Ticket system example"],"rows":[["Tool","An action has a side effect, or output depends heavily on model supplied arguments","create_ticket, add_comment, search_tickets"],["Resource","The model just needs to read context, with little or no meaningful input needed","ticket by id, current queue backlog"],["Prompt","A workflow benefits from a consistent, reusable template","draft_customer_reply, triage_new_ticket"]]}

blocks.text: A quick test: if invoking it does something, or its output depends nontrivially on an argument, it is a tool. Otherwise it is probably a resource.
5. Designing Tool Schemas

blocks.alt: A tool schema is designed with required and optional fields

blocks.text: A tool schema is a contract, and a sloppy one is where most real bugs in MCP servers start.
Prefer enums and typed fields over free text wherever the underlying system already enforces a fixed set of values.
Notice priority and queue are enums, not free text, because the ticketing system already enforces a fixed set of valid values.
6. Designing Resources and Their URIs
Resources need a stable, predictable naming scheme so a client can request one directly without guessing.
A consistent scheme like this also makes pagination and filtering easier to bolt on later without breaking existing callers.
7. Error Handling and Validation
Validate every input against the schema before it ever reaches the underlying system, and fail fast with a structured, typed error.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Failure type","What the server should return"],"rows":[["Bad input, fails schema","A validation error naming the exact field, no side effect performed"],["Underlying system rejects the request","A typed error mapped from the underlying failure, not a raw stack trace"],["Underlying system times out","A retryable error, distinct from a permanent one, so the client knows whether to retry"],["Caller lacks permission","A clear authorization error, never a silent empty result"]]}

blocks.text: The goal is that a client can always tell the difference between try again later and this will never work, without parsing free text.
8. Authentication and Access Control

blocks.alt: A request passes authentication then an access control check before it proceeds

blocks.text: Decide early whose identity a call runs as, the end user, a service account, or something in between.
Forwarding the caller's own credential into the underlying system is usually the strongest default, since it inherits that system's existing permission model for free.

items: Authenticate the MCP client connection itself before anything else happens
Forward or map that identity onto the underlying system's own authorization checks
Scope every tool as narrowly as the task actually needs, never grant a whole schema for one lookup

blocks.text: Skipping this until the interviewer asks about security is one of the fastest ways to look like you have only read about MCP, not built with it.
9. State, Sessions, and Idempotency

blocks.alt: State, sessions, and idempotency are three design concerns for a server

blocks.text: Prefer a stateless server wherever possible, since it scales horizontally without any extra coordination.
Where state is unavoidable, such as a long running search cursor, store it in the underlying system or a shared cache, never pinned to one process.
Give any tool with a side effect an idempotency key, so a client retry after a timeout cannot accidentally create a duplicate ticket.
10. Scaling and Performance

blocks.alt: A single instance scales out into a fleet behind a load balancer

blocks.text: A stateless design means scaling is mostly about adding more instances behind a load balancer, nothing more exotic.
Watch the underlying system's own limits closely, since a fast MCP layer in front of a rate limited API is still rate limited.

items: Cache read heavy resources that change slowly, like a queue list refreshed once a minute
Batch or paginate any tool call that could otherwise return thousands of rows at once
Apply your own rate limiting per caller so one noisy client cannot starve everyone else

blocks.text: 11. Observability and Operations
Log every tool call with its caller identity, arguments, latency, and outcome, since this is what makes an incident reviewable afterward.
Emit metrics per tool, call volume, error rate, and latency, so a regression in one tool never hides inside an average across the whole server.

blocks.title: Treat logs as an audit trail
blocks.content: A model can take real actions on a user's behalf, so the log of what it called and why should be as trustworthy as any other production audit trail.

blocks.text: 12. Versioning and Evolving the Contract

blocks.alt: An old contract version is compared against a new one during evolution

blocks.text: Treat tool and resource schemas as a public contract, since existing clients keep calling them long after you ship a change.
Add new optional fields freely, but never repurpose an existing field's meaning or silently remove one clients depend on.
For a breaking change, ship a new tool name or a new resource path alongside the old one, then deprecate the old one on a clear timeline.
Worked Example, a Support Ticket MCP Server
The prompt: design an MCP server that lets an internal AI assistant help support agents work a ticket queue.
Requirements Recap
Clients are internal support agents using one company approved AI assistant, so this stays inside a trusted network, not the open internet.

items: Read access, viewing tickets, searching the queue, reading a customer's history
Write access, creating tickets, adding comments, and changing ticket status
Scale is modest today, roughly two hundred agents, but should not require a redesign at two thousand

blocks.text: Resources We Expose
Anything the assistant only needs to read becomes a resource, addressed through the stable URI scheme from section six.

code.content:
tickets://ticket/{id}              a single ticket with its full history
tickets://ticket/{id}/comments      the comment thread on one ticket
tickets://queue/{name}/backlog      open tickets waiting in one queue

blocks.text: Tools We Expose
Anything that changes state, or needs meaningful model supplied input to be useful, becomes a tool.
create_ticket from section five and search_tickets, which takes a query string plus optional status and priority filters, round out the tool set.
Prompts We Expose
One reusable prompt earns its place here, draft_customer_reply, which bakes in the company's tone and structure for a first response.
Agents invoke it with a ticket id, and get back a consistent, on brand draft they can edit rather than write from a blank page each time.
Auth and Access Control
Every call forwards the agent's existing single sign on token, so the underlying ticketing API applies its own per agent permissions.
The MCP server itself adds nothing new here, it simply refuses to strip or bypass whatever authorization header the client already sends.
Error Handling in Practice

blocks.content: {"headers":["Situation","Response"],"rows":[["Ticket id does not exist","A typed not found error, never a silently empty result"],["Comment body exceeds the length limit","A validation error naming the field, before any write happens"],["Agent lacks permission for a queue","A typed authorization error, mirroring the underlying API's own check"]]}

blocks.text: Scaling and Observability Choices
Since it is internal and stateless, a small pool of servers behind the existing company load balancer is enough on day one.
Every call is logged with agent id, tool name, ticket id, and latency, feeding the same dashboards the ticketing team already watches.
Putting It Together
That is a complete, defensible answer, built in the same order every time regardless of the specific domain named in the prompt.

blocks.text: Common Mistakes

items: Jumping straight to tool names before clarifying who the caller is and what scale is expected
Turning every capability into a tool, including plain lookups that would be cleaner as resources
Using vague free text fields where the underlying system already enforces a fixed set of values
Forgetting authentication and authorization entirely until the interviewer asks about security
Assuming horizontal scaling works without checking whether state is accidentally pinned to one process
Treating the first schema as permanent, with no plan for how a breaking change would ever roll out

blocks.text: Practice
Take the prompt, design an MCP server for a company internal wiki, and walk through every section above out loud, ideally recorded.

items: Decide which capabilities become tools, which become resources, and whether any prompt earns a place
Sketch one full tool schema in json the way this lesson did for create_ticket and add_comment
Stretch goal, revise your auth design assuming external contractors now need more limited access than employees

blocks.text: Key Takeaway

This question rewards a repeatable process more than domain trivia, clarify scope, sort capabilities into tools, resources, and prompts, then design schemas, auth, scaling, and observability in that order.
Walk through the same sequence every time, whether the prompt is about tickets, calendars, or code, and a nervous improvisation turns into a confident, structured answer.
